summary: Extends the SIP REFER method to use caller preferences from RFC 3840, so the sender of a REFER can describe the characteristics of the target that the induced request should reach. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When asking a friend to call someone for you, you can also say what kind of phone to reach, like the mobile.

questions: how does refer-to carry feature tags
subtitle: How the sender of a SIP REFER can tell the recipient what the referred-to party can do.

tldr.problem: A SIP REFER asks one party to contact a third party, but the recipient does not know the third party's capabilities, such as whether it supports video or is a conference host.
tldr.mechanism: The REFER-Issuer may add feature tags from RFC 3840 as parameters on the Refer-To header field, describing the REFER-Target.
tldr.outcome: The recipient can tailor the request it sends, but must treat the tags as hints because they cannot be authenticated from the REFER itself. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8217.

today: RFC 4508 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8217. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Feature Tags Help a REFER
sections.content:
RFC 4508 extends the SIP REFER method from RFC 3515 so that it can carry the feature parameters defined in RFC 3840. Feature tags are how a user agent (UA) tells another UA about its capabilities and features.

Feature tag information can already be shared through REGISTER requests and responses, OPTIONS responses, or the remote target (Contact) URI inside a dialog. The RFC says this information is especially useful before a session is established. If a UA knows the remote UA supports both video and audio, it can offer video in the SDP when it calls.

The new mechanism lets the party sending the REFER pass along what it knows about the party to be contacted, by putting feature tags in the Refer-To header field.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you call someone, it helps to know what kind of phone they have. This lets a person who knows pass that along when asking you to make the call.

sections.title: Three Roles in a REFER
sections.content:
To keep the discussion clear, the RFC defines three terms.

  • REFER-Issuer: the UA issuing the REFER request.
  • REFER-Recipient: the UA receiving the REFER request.
  • REFER-Target: the UA designated in the Refer-To URI.

The Issuer describes the Target to the Recipient. The Recipient is then expected to send the induced request to the Target.
sections.plainLanguage: There is the person who asks, the person who is asked, and the person who gets called. The asker tells the helper about the person to be called.

sections.title: The Extended Refer-To Header
sections.content:
RFC 3515 defines Refer-To as a name-address or address-spec followed by any number of generic parameters. RFC 4508 replaces the generic parameter with a refer-param, which is either a generic-param or a feature-param. The feature-param is the one defined in Section 9 of RFC 3840.

One syntax detail matters. If any URI parameters are present, the entire URI must be enclosed in < and >. Without the angle brackets, every parameter after the URI is a header parameter, not a URI parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The address line now has room for little labels about the person at that address. If the address itself has extras, you have to wrap it in brackets so the labels do not get mixed up with it.

sections.title: Examples in the RFC
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples.

  • The isfocus tag tells the Recipient that the Target is a conference focus, so sending an INVITE will bring the Recipient into the conference.
  • The audio and video tags tell the Recipient that the Target supports both, so a video and audio session can be established by sending an INVITE.
  • A voicemail server is described with actor="msg-taker", automata and audio. The transport=tcp URI parameter sits inside the angle brackets so it is not read as a header parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say the person is a conference host, that they have a video phone, or that they are an answering machine. Each is a small tag stuck onto the address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Feature tags can reveal sensitive information about a user or UA. RFC 3840 cautions against giving such information to another party, and once it is given out, any use may be made of it, including relaying it to a third party as this specification does.

A REFER-Issuer MUST NOT create or guess feature tags. A tag in a REFER SHOULD be discovered in an authenticated and secure way, such as an OPTIONS response or the remote target URI in a dialog, directly from the REFER-Target. It is RECOMMENDED that the Issuer include all feature tags from the Target's most recent Contact header field.

The Recipient cannot authenticate a tag from the REFER itself, so it MUST treat the information as a hint. If its logic or the user's action depends on the feature, it can verify it, for example by sending an OPTIONS query to the Target over a secure, mutually authenticated and integrity-protected connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Treat what you are told as a hint, not a promise. If it really matters, ask the person directly in a safe way.
